input.quote: (ii) Either Party may, without consent of the other Party, assign this Agreement in whole to (i) in the case of RevMed, its successor in interest or assignee or purchaser, as applicable, in the case of a Change of Control or (ii) in the case of Sanofi, its successor in interest or assignee or purchaser, as applicable, in connection with the sale of all or substantially all of its assets to which this Agreement relates, or in connection with a merger, acquisition or similar transaction.
input.rationale: Section 15.2 gives us (Sanofi) exactly the carve-outs the playbook asks for: we may assign to any Affiliate without RevMed's consent (15.2(a)(i)) and may assign the whole Agreement, without consent, to a successor in a sale of all or substantially all relevant assets or in a merger, acquisition or similar transaction (15.2(a)(ii)). The restriction is not asymmetric against us — RevMed's Affiliate assignments require our consent (not to be unreasonably withheld, delayed or conditioned), its licensed-Patent transfers to Third Parties require our consent (15.2(b)), and any Acquiror-side assignment is fenced by the Acquiror Family/Acquired Party Family firewall conditions (A)–(D). Nothing gives RevMed a right to terminate, re-price or re-open the deal on a change of control of Sanofi: the only change-of-control termination right in Article XII runs in our favour (Section 12.2(a)(ii), on a Change of Control of RevMed), and RevMed's termination rights (material breach, insolvency, Competing Product, cessation of development) are not CoC-triggered. Two sub-elements fall short of the ideal preferred wording but are not material deviations and are noted only: (i) RevMed's successor assignment on its own Change of Control is not consent-gated and there is no express bar on assignment to a Sanofi competitor — mitigated by our 12.2(a)(ii) termination option and the Major Biopharmaceutical Company treatment; and (ii) Section 12.3 (p0508) cuts off RevMed's post-termination royalties to us upon a Change of Control of Sanofi, which is back-end termination economics rather than a vendor exit or re-pricing right under this rule and is better addressed under the termination-effects rule. On its material terms the clause meets the preferred position, so no redline.
